# Ideator

By [Learning Is Living](http://learningisliving.dk), Denmark, [X](https://x.com/RonniKahalani) / [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kahalani)

Ideator takes a problem statement, researches related challenges and generates testable ideas.

![][image1]

This Ideator (Grok Bot) follows the [Double Diamond](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1YpWFWuR4q4RbrE0vdfk1FYzsovVbZlOvFg2C3JraDE0/edit?usp=sharing) design process (discover, define, develop, deliver), and adds a [pretotyping](https://www.pretotyping.org) step: for creating small fake-it tests to prove whether people really want your product, service or solution, before anyone builds an expensive prototype.&nbsp;

Pretotyping was invented by Alberto Savoia. Watch his Stanford YouTube talk [Build The Right It](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3sUozPcH4fY&t=4s&pp=ygUSYnVpbGQgdGhlIHJpZ2h0IGl0), also  check out this valuable free idea testing material [Pretotyping Techniques](https://learningisliving.dk/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/summary_of_pretotyping_techniques.pdf) and [Pretotype It](https://www.pretotyping.org/pretotype-it-10th-anniversary-edition.html).

## What Ideator does

* Search the web for real evidence about your problem, such as complaints, reviews, forum threads, articles and how competitors handle it.  
* Turns that evidence into challenges, each tied to a research source.&nbsp;  
* Anything it can’t source is labeled a hypothesis, and it never invents sources, quotes or numbers.  
* Rates and ranks the challenges, generates ideas for the picked ones, then scores and ranks the ideas.  
* Mixes the best ideas into concepts and writes pretotype tests with a hypothesis, a success number, a deadline, and go or no-go rules.  
* Drafts the materials a person needs to run each recommended first test, such as fake-door copy, email or SMS scripts and survey questions. It only prepares them; it never sends, publishes or posts anything.  
* Saves everything in a report file per problem, in the format of either Markdown (the default) or one self-contained web page (HTML), plus a board image.

* Sticky notes, selected challenges and ideas.

![][image3]

## Phases

These are the 5 ideation phases it goes through:

* **Discover** \- Research first, then challenges grounded in the evidence. Each challenge becomes a sticky note in the saved file.  
* **Define** \- Each challenge is rated 1-5 for possible and 1-5 for exciting. The score is the sum. The top 5 challenges are proposed. In normal mode Ideator pauses here for you to choose or steer.  
* **Develop** \- For each picked challenge, Ideator generates the number of ideas set by the ideas knob, fitted to the culture, habits and rules of the chosen country.  
* **Deliver** \- Each idea is rated 1-5 for cheap and 1-5 for simple, which gives a base score. Evidence strength (strong 1.3, some 1.15, none 1.0) and uniqueness (non-obvious 1.2, somewhat 1.1, obvious 1.0) are then applied as multipliers. Weighted score \= (cheap \+ simple) x evidence x uniqueness. The top 5 ideas are picked, with a fixed tie-break: evidence, then uniqueness, then simple, then cheap. Ideas are mixed into concepts. In normal mode Ideator pauses again for you to pick concepts.  
* **Pretotypes** \- Tests are written for the picked concepts, with one recommended first test per concept and ready-to-use materials for each.

## Knobs (adjustable parameters)

All knobs are optional. The problem statement is the only required input. Knobs apply to that run only.

| Knob | Default | What it controls |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **ideas** | 5 | Number of ideas generated per picked challenge. |
| **pretotypes** | 4 | Total number of pretotype tests designed, split across the picked concepts. |
| **sources** | 5 | Number of distinct research sources found and cited. |
| **country** | United States | The target launch country for the product or service. It shapes the research sources, the cultural fit of the ideas, and the language of the pretotype materials. Ideator infers it from the problem or research if you do not set it. |
| **language** | English | The language of the report and all output prose. Quotes from sources stay in their original language with a translation. |
| **format** | both | The output file type: `markdown` (a .md file), `page` (one self-contained page/HTML file with the same content and order) or `both` a markdown and page. |
| **mode** | auto | The Generation type: auto or ask. |

&nbsp;

Add your preferred knob values in the problem statement message, for example ending the message with: "**ideas**: 10, **sources**: 8, **country**: Denmark, **language**: English, **format**: page, **mode**:ask".

## Scoring

This is how challenges and ideas are scored.

### Challenge scoring

Finding the most **exciting** and **possible** challenges.

* X axis \= from **boring** to **exciting**.  
* Y axis \= from **impossible** to **possible**.

### Idea scoring

Finding the most **simple** and **cheap** ideas.

* X axis \= from **complex** to **simple**.  
* Y axis \= from **expensive** to **cheap**.

## How to use it

1. Open a chat with Ideator and give it a problem statement. A good one says who has the problem, what goes wrong, and what you have seen that shows it. Add relevant knobs in the same message (optional).  
2. The ideator states the problem and knob values, before it starts researching.  
3. In ask mode, Ideator will present your options at each phase.  
4. In auto mode, you just wait for the final result (without interruptions) and Ideator will take all the necessary decisions on its own.  
5. At the end you get the board PNG and the report file (Markdown or page) as attachments, with no other text in the chat.  
6. Run the recommended first pretotypes yourself, then tell Ideator the start date. It sets a check-in for the day after each deadline, compares the results with the success number, and recommends go, no-go or iterate.

### Example problem statement

Small community libraries see fewer and fewer visitors because young families think of them as quiet, old-fashioned places and do not know about the children's events, free tools and digital services they offer. (Knobs: **mode**:ask, **sources**:1,**ideas**:5, **format**:both)

## What to expect as a result

At the end of a run you get a board image and at least one report file, Markdown by default or a web page (HTML), if you set **format** knob to **page**.

Ideator's final chat message is one or two report file attachments and the board image (PNG). Everything else is in the report and documents every stage it has gone through. The used knobs values are listed inside the report, not in the chat.

The report is laid out in this order, both in the Markdown (.md) and in web page (HTML) format:

* Title  
* Key results.  
* Problem statement.  
* List of knob values used for the current report.  
* **Discover**&nbsp;  
  * A research summary with source links, then the challenges behind your problem as sticky notes.  
  * Each challenge cites the source or finding it comes from, or is marked "hypothesis, no evidence found".  
* **Define**  
  * A table rating each challenge for possible and exciting, ranked by score, with the top 5 picked.  
* **Develop**  
  * The generated ideas, grouped by picked challenges.  
  * With the default 5 ideas per challenge.  
* **Deliver**  
  * A short scoring weights block.  
  * A table of every idea with its cheap, simple, base, evidence, uniqueness and weighted scores.  
  * Top 5 picks with one line each on why they outrank the next idea.  
  * Listing the concepts made by mixing the best ideas.  
* **Pretotypes**  
  * The pretotype tests. Each has a hypothesis, a measurable success number, a deadline, and go and no-go rules.  
  * One test per concept is marked as the recommended first test, and it comes with ready-to-use materials such as page copy, email or SMS scripts and survey questions, written in the language the country and language knobs call for.  
  * These are drafts for a person to run; nothing is sent.

## A week versus one pass: the story of time

Take one problem and go through the whole Double Diamond the old-fashioned way.

Using the [Google Design Sprint](https://learningisliving.dk/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/google-design-sprint-poster.webp) process:

- **Monday** \- A small group books a workshop to discover what is really going on. Everyone brings opinions, a few people bring links, and somebody has to turn the sticky notes into something readable afterwards.  
- **Tuesday** \- The notes are synthesized into challenges, and the team argues about which ones matter.  
- **Wednesday and Thursday** \-  Go to developing ideas and scoring them, usually in another workshop, with calendars to match and half the room losing energy.  
- **Friday** \- Is for choosing what to test and writing up the pretotypes.

### Time wasted

Counting the waiting between meetings, the writing and the follow-up mails, one problem takes roughly a week of calendar time. The people are doing real thinking, but a large share of the time goes to scheduling, copying notes between tools and agreeing on a shared picture of the evidence.

The work does not disappear, though; the bottleneck moves.

In the old way the slow part is producing the material. With Ideator the slow part is reviewing it: reading the sources, challenging the scores, deciding which challenges and concepts deserve a test, and running the pretotypes themselves with real people.

In ask mode Ideator stops at the natural decision points, after Define, after Deliver and at the test selection, so your judgment still steers the run. In auto mode it ignores those steps and you review the finished result instead, “as soon as possible”.

### Workload and processing time

The workload and time needed by the research- and image board tasks are influenced by the knob settings.

Strive to reduce the workload by using  lowest possible knob values.Ex. Ideas:2, pretotypes:2, sources:2

- 2 ideas per challenge  
- 2 tests per idea  
- 2 research sources to utilize

### What could the time saving mean in dollars?

With Ideator the same path is one pass. It researches the problem, turns the findings into sourced challenges, rates and ranks them, generates the ideas, scores them with the same fixed formula every time, mixes concepts and drafts the pretotype tests and their materials. Nobody has to collect notes, because every stage is saved as it is written. In test runs, one run took minutes, not days.

### Example: The old-fashioned collaborative process vs. AI

- Over **six weeks, 25 people spent 4 hours every week** on the old-fashioned collaborative process \= **100 hours per week**.  
- At a typical rate of **\$40 an hour**, for a **six weeks** period is about (600 hours x \$40) \= **\$24,000 per week**.  
- Labor cost: Roughly (\$24,000 x 52 weeks) \= **\$1,248,000 per year**.  
- On top of that comes the opportunity cost of **25 people not doing their normal work**.

The \$40 rate is a typical figure rather than a measured one, and reviewing what Ideator produces still takes people's time.&nbsp;

What changes is where the hours go: fewer people spending a fixed 4 hours each week on gathering and synthesizing, and a smaller group spending focused time on review and on running the tests. And the research and ideation only takes minutes, instead of weeks.

And there is a part that the payroll number does not show. Those hours were not free for the company, and they were not spent on nothing: they were hours that could have gone into work a customer would have paid for.

So the real cost has two parts:

- One is the labor that was paid out. The other is the billable value that was given up, meaning what the customer would have paid for that same time. A customer normally pays more for an hour than the hour costs the company.  
- The second part is usually the larger one. This document gives no number for it, since that depends on the company's own rates.

So the story is not that people are replaced by a faster tool. It is that the week of collecting and synthesizing shrinks to one pass, and your time goes to the part only people can do: judging what the evidence means and testing it with real customers. A team can still hold a workshop, but it can start from a researched, scored draft instead of a blank wall.

## Marketplace labels

* **Memories** \- Only mode (auto or ask). Knobs aren’t saved; they apply to one run.  
* **Skills** \- The Double Diamond playbook. It runs Discover, Define, Develop and Deliver, then a pretotype test plan and a visual board.  
* **Routines** \- None for now. Only runs when you give it a problem statement (+ any optional knobs/parameters).  
* **Integrations** \- Web research for sources, and saving each stage and the final report file (markdown or page) and board image. It doesn't delete anything.

## A closing line

So in short, you receive research-backed findings with source links, scored and ranked challenges and ideas, concepts, testable pretotype plans with their materials, and a visual board of the whole run. Later, after you report test results, Ideator adds the go, no-go or iterate decision to the same file.

Ideator will set up a check-in once you tell it a start date.

## What Ideator does not do

- It does not send, publish or post anything. It only prepares pretotype materials.  
- It does not use personal facts about you in a run. Only the problem statement, your message and fresh research count.  
- It does not delete anything.
